ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A silicon photocell is a kind of solar cell and has the advantages of being low-carbon and environmentally friendly. As shown in Figure 12, curve a is the graph of the relationship between the terminal voltage U and current I of this cell under a certain light intensity (the internal resistance of the cell is not constant), and line b is the U-I graph of a certain resistor R. When they are connected to form a closed circuit under this light intensity, what is the internal resistance of the silicon photocell?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the vertical axis is terminal voltage U/V, and the horizontal axis is current I/A. Curve a is the U-I relationship curve of the silicon photocell; when I=0, it intersects the vertical axis at U=3.6 V, namely the open-circuit voltage is 3.6 V. Straight line b is the U-I graph of resistor R; it passes through the origin and intersects curve a; the dashed lines in the figure mark the intersection coordinates as I=0.2 A and U=2.5 V. Then reasoning: When the silicon photocell and resistor R are connected to form a closed circuit, the actual working current and terminal voltage are determined by the intersection of the two U-I graphs, so the working point is I=0.2 A and U=2.5 V. When open-circuited, the current is 0 and the internal voltage drop is 0, so the electromotive force E of the cell equals the open-circuit voltage 3.6 V. During operation, the internal voltage drop is E-U=3.6-2.5=1.1 V. The equivalent internal resistance of the silicon photocell in this working state is r=(E-U)/I=1.1/0.2=5.5 Ω.
